Another rare plant, Oconee bells (Shortia galacifolia), (Figure 2-24), commonly found in ravines along moist hill sides throughout the area (Davies, 1955) is on the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service (1976) proposed list of endangered plants. This plant was encountered along the proposed transmission line right-of-way during the botanical survey. It is thought that this plant was first found by Andre Michaux during the 18th century at the junction of the Horsepasture and Toxaway Rivers. This area, considered to have been near the center of distribution of this species, was flooded when Lake Jocassee was formed (Davies, 1955). Oconee bells grow best in acid humus along streams shaded by rhododendron or other shrubs or trees.
Many plant species of rare or uncommon status found in the southeast have been identified by the U.S. Forest Service (1970) and some of threatened status have been identified by the Smithsonian Institution (1975). Threatened plant species are those that are presently not endangered but are likely to become so within the foreseeable future throughout all or a significant portion of their range. Rare plant species are extremely scarce throughout their range, or may be quite abundant where they do occur, but grow in only a few localities. Uncommon species are those whose abundance is somewhat greater than rare species. The following plant species have threatened, rare, or uncommon status and ranges encompassing the project area:
